items.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: to work with McKenna, you know, beautiful. Then we added Bob Wilber and Cutty Cutshall and we went out and we always had that good quartet

ctx.x: How does it change your playing to work without a bass player?

Well you adjust the playing. Sometimes I just leave the hi hat off. And you play off the snare and the bass drum stays very steady. You’ve got to re-tune it where it gets a nice tone. And it all depends on that piano player see? You’ve got to have a nice, loose left © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

hand. Can’t be pounding. Teddy can play you know. There’s only one Teddy Wilson. And that’s Johnny Varro. But Johnny is very good, absolutely. And Ralph Sutton. We have a good, easy time with Ralph and we have an easy time with John Bunch, and Dave McKenna, he’s born for that, Dave McKenna is the king of that stuff. In fact he doesn’t need us. So the hell with Dave.

items.title: Dave McKenna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: I did a record date with him for a Japanese label in June in New York, with Michael Moore and Jake Hanna, there was four of us.

ctx.x: Well I like some of your album titles too, they’re creative. You had “No Bass Hit”—

I think that was, I’ve got to give Carl Jefferson credit. I think he came up with that and “Major League.” Those were the two with — “No Bass Hit” was the first one with Concord, and that was with Jake and Scott. And then I did a solo album shortly after, and “Major League” was a few years later, and for Concord I did a trio album playing that Harry Warren music, and I did an album with Gray Sargent, a duo; and an album with Joe Temperley, a duo; an album with Buddy DeFranco, a duo; a lot of duos; plus the things…
You had mentioned that there was a time in your life when you were thinking about the post office. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
